---
<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
Given an odd natural number $n$, define a graph $G_n = (V, E)$ as follows:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item The vertex set is 
		\[
		V = \{1, 2, \dotsc, (n-1)/2\}.
		\]
		\item The edge set $E \subseteq V \times V$ consists of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ such that
		\[
		b \equiv \pm 2a \pmod{n}.
		\]
	\end{itemize}
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
\label{defn of On}
Given any odd natural number $n$, we let $\mathcal{O}(n)$ denote the number of  cycles of odd length in $G_n$, where a loop is considered a cycle of length 1.
For convenience, we put $\mathcal{O}(1) = 0$.
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\cite[Prop.\,1]{FLS} \label{tight equi-diff prop}
Given an odd integer $n \geq 3$, a tight equi-difference code $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{CAC}^{e}(n)$ exists if and only if $3\nmid n$ and  $\mathcal{O}(n) = 0$, or $3\mid n$ and $\mathcal{O}(n) = 1$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{tight equi code thm}
Let $P(x)$ and $N(x)$ denote the number of primes, respectively odd integers $1\le n\le x$, for which a tight equi-difference code of length $n$ exists.
We have
\[
P(x)=\frac{5}{12}\frac{x}{\log x}+O\Bigl(\frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^{7/6}}\Bigr)\quad\text{~and~}\quad
N(x)=C\frac{x}{(\log x)^{7/12}}+O\Bigl(\frac{x(\log\log x)^5}{(\log x)^{19/12}}\Bigr),
\]
with $C$ a positive constant. 
More precisely, if $C_{0}$ denotes the constant appearing in Theorem \ref{density O(m) is zero thm}, then $C=\frac{4}{3}C_{0}\approx 0.4298\dotsc$
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{main}
Let $k \ge 1$ be an integer.
The set of primes $P_k$ has a natural density $\delta_k$ given by
$$
\delta_k =
A\cdot E(k) \cdot
\begin{cases}
1 & \ \textrm{if}\ k{\text~is~odd};\\
0 & \ \textrm{if}\ k\equiv 2\pmod{4};\\
2/3 & \ \textrm{if}\ 4\mid k,
\end{cases}
$$
with
\begin{equation*}
\label{Artinconstantdef}
A\coloneq \prod_{\textrm{prime $q$}}\Big (1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)} \Big) = 0.3739558136192022880547280543464\dotsc,
\end{equation*} 
the Artin constant and
\begin{equation}
\label{def:Ek}    
E(k)\coloneq \frac{1}{k^2}\prod_{q\mid k}\frac{q^2-1}{q^2-q-1}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, asymptotically in $x$,
\[  P_k(x) = \delta_k \frac{x}{\log x} + O_{k}\Big(\frac{x\log\log x}{\log^2x} \Big). \]
In case $k\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, we have $P_k(x)=0$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:p1ad}
Let $a$ and $d$ be coprime positive integers. 
Under  GRH, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:underGRH}
P_1(a,d)(x)= 
\frac{\rho(d,a)}{\varphi(d)}\frac{x}{\log x}
+
O_d\Bigl(\frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^{2}}\Bigr),
\end{equation}
with
$$
\rho(d,a)=c(d,a)R(d,a)A,
$$
where
\[
R(d,a)\coloneq 2\prod_{p\mid (a-1,d)}\Big(1-\frac{1}{p}\Big)
\prod_{p\mid d}\Big(1+\frac{1}{p^2-p-1}\Big),
\]
and
$$
c(d,a)\coloneq 
\begin{cases}1/2  & \textrm{if~}4\nmid d;\\
1  & \textrm{if~}4\mid d,~a\equiv 3 \pmod{4};\\
0  & \textrm{if~}4\mid d,~a\equiv 1 \pmod{4}.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{CAC-prime-values thm}
Let $p$ be an odd prime such that $\mathcal{O}(p)$ is an odd prime. Then the upper bound in \eqref{M(p) ineq} is attained, and hence
\[
M(p)=M^{e}(p)+\Bigl\lfloor\frac{\mathcal{O}(p)}{3}\Bigr\rfloor=\frac{p-1}{4}
-\frac{\mathcal{O}(p)}{2}+\Bigl\lfloor\frac{\mathcal{O}(p)}{3}\Bigr\rfloor.
\]
Moreover, assuming GRH, the set of such primes has relative density $0.508822711238\dotsc$ within the set of odd primes $p$ satisfying $\mathcal{O}(p)>2$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{density O(m) is zero thm}
For $x\geq 3$ and $e\ge 0$, let 
\[
N_{e}(x) \coloneq \#\{1 < m \leq x:m \ \textrm{odd and} \ \mathcal{O}(m)=e\}.
\]
We have
\[
N_{0}(x)=C_{0}\frac{x}{(\log x)^{7/12}}
+O\Bigl(
\frac{x(\log\log x)^5}{(\log x)^{19/12}}
\Bigr),
\]
with $$C_0=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\frac{5}{12})}\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty}\prod_{p\le t}
g(p)\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{p}\Bigr)^{\frac{5}{12}}=0.32235\dotsc,$$
and $g(p)=(1-1/p)^{-1}$ if $2\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ and $g(p)=1$ otherwise.
For every fixed $e\ge 1$ and for sufficiently large $x$, we have  
$$N_e(x)
\gg_{e} \frac{x}{(\log x)^{7/12}}.$$
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
\label{mult ord def}
Let $a\in \mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ and $n\ge 2$. Assume that $\nu_p(a)=0$ for every prime $p\mid n$; equivalently, if $a=r/s$ is written in lowest terms, then $\gcd(rs,n)=1$. The reduction of $a$ modulo $n$ is then the element $
\overline{a}:=r s^{-1}\in (\mathbb{Z}_{n})^{\times}$. Then the smallest integer $k\ge 1$ such that $\overline{a}^k\equiv 1\pmod{n}$ is called the \emph{multiplicative order} of $a$ modulo $n$ and denoted by $\operatorname{ord}_n(a)$. Differently phrased it is the order of the subgroup $\langle \overline{a}\rangle$ generated by $\overline{a}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{\times}$. The index of that subgroup is denoted by $\operatorname{ind}_n(a)$ and called the \emph{index} of $a$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{\times}$. We have
$$\operatorname{ind}_n(a)=\frac{\varphi(n)}{\operatorname{ord}_n(a)}.$$
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{thm-FLS}
For odd $n \geq 3$, we have 
$$\mathcal{O}(n)=\sum_{d\, \mid \, n} \delta_{d},$$
where
$$
\delta_{d}=
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ind}_d(2) & \ \textrm{if}\ \operatorname{ord}_d(2)\textrm{~is~odd~and~} >1;\\[1ex]
\operatorname{ind}_d(2) & \ \textrm{if}\ \operatorname{ord}_d(2) \equiv 2 \pmod{4}, \ 2^{\operatorname{ord}_d(2)/2}\equiv-1\pmod{d};\\[1ex]
0 & \textrm{~otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:ord4-formula}
For every odd integer $n\geq 3$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{O(n) defn interms ord of 4}
    \mathcal{O}(n)=\sum_{\substack{d\, \mid \, n, \ d >1 \\ 2\,\nmid\, \operatorname{ord}_{d}(4)\\ 2^{\operatorname{ord}_d(4)}\equiv\pm1\pmod{d}}} \frac{\varphi(d)}{2\operatorname{ord}_{d}(4)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Identify the vertices of $G_n$ with the nonzero residue classes modulo
$n$, up to sign.  For each divisor $d>1$ of $n$, let
\[
  \Omega_n(d)\coloneq \left\{[a]\in (\mathbb{Z} _n\setminus\{0\})/\{\pm1\}:\frac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}=d\right\}.
\]
The set $\Omega_n(d)$ has $\varphi(d)/2$ elements and is invariant under the map $[a]\mapsto[2a]$.  Every cycle contained in $\Omega_n(d)$ has length $s_d\coloneq \min\{r\geq1:2^r\equiv\pm1\pmod{d}\}$. Put $q_d=\operatorname{ord}_d(4)$. Since $4^{q_d}\equiv1\pmod{d}$, we have $2^{2q_d}\equiv1\pmod{d}$, and hence $s_d\mid 2q_d$. Conversely, if $2^r\equiv\pm1\pmod{d}$, then $4^r\equiv1\pmod{d}$;
therefore $q_d\mid r$.  It follows that
\[
  s_d=
  \begin{cases}
     q_d,  & \text{if }2^{q_d}\equiv\pm1\pmod{d},\\
     2q_d, & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]
Consequently, the cycles contained in $\Omega_n(d)$ have odd length if
and only if $q_d$ is odd and $2^{q_d}\equiv\pm1\pmod{d}$. When these conditions hold, $\Omega_n(d)$ consists of
\[
  \frac{|\Omega_n(d)|}{q_d}=\frac{\varphi(d)}{2q_d}
\]
odd cycles.  Summing over the divisors $d>1$ of $n$, we obtain \eqref{O(n) defn interms ord of 4}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
\label{firstremark}
The congruence condition in \eqref{O(n) defn interms ord of 4} is not redundant
for composite $d$, since the congruence $x^2\equiv1\pmod{d}$ may have
solutions other than $x\equiv\pm1\pmod{d}$.  When $d=p$ is an odd prime,
however, the condition is automatic.  Thus
\[
  \mathcal{O}(p)=
  \begin{cases}
  \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ind}_p(4),
      & \text{if $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is odd};\\[8pt]
  0,  & \text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\]
The graph-theoretic meaning of this prime-length specialization will be
developed in the next section.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
Let $n$ be a natural number. Define a graph $H_n = (V, E)$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
	\item The vertex set $V$ is the set of non-zero squares in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$, i.e.,
	\[
	V = \{ x^2 \pmod{n} : x \in \mathbb{Z}_n \} \setminus \{0\}.
	\]
	\item The edge set $E \subseteq V \times V$ consists of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ such that
	\[
	b \equiv 4a \pmod{n}.
	\]
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
Let $p\geq 3$ be a prime.
Then $G_p$ and $H_p$ are isomorphic as directed graphs.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Define the map 
\[
\phi  \colon  V(G_p) \to V(H_p) \quad \textrm{by} \quad \phi(a) = a^2 \pmod{p}.
\]
Since $p$ is prime, it implies that there are only two elements  $a, p-a \in \mathbb{Z}_{p} \setminus \{0\}$  whose square is equal to $a^2$.
Therefore, the map $\phi  \colon  V(G_p) \to V(H_p) $ is injective and surjective.
Now, suppose that there is a directed edge $a \to b$ in $G_p$. Then $b \equiv \pm 2a \pmod{p}$. Consider
\[
\phi(b) = b^2 \equiv (\pm 2a)^2 = 4a^2 \equiv 4 \phi(a) \pmod{p},
\]
so that there is an edge from $\phi(a)$ to $\phi(b)$ in $H_p$.
Hence, $\phi$ is a homomorphism of graphs.

In order to see that $\phi$ is a graph isomorphism, we only need to prove that whenever there is an edge between  $\phi(a) $  and $\phi(b)$, there is an edge between $a$ and $b$. 
 If $(\phi(a),\phi(b)) \in E(H_p)$,
 then $b^2-4a^2\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ and 
 hence either $p\mid b+2a  $ or $p\mid b-2a $. Thus, there is an edge connecting  $a$ and $b$ in the graph $G_p$.
Hence, $\phi$ is a graph isomorphism from $G_p$ to $H_p$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
If $ n $ is not a prime number, then
$G_n$ is not necessarily isomorphic 
to $H_n$. Even in the case where $ n $ is squarefree, several challenges arise, namely:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The sets of vertices in the corresponding graphs may not be identical in size.
        \item The  congruence $ x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{n} $ can have up to $ 2^{\omega(n)} $ solutions, which may result in the presence of edges in $ H_n $ that do not appear in $ G_n$ (as usual $\omega(n)$ denotes the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$).
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{no of odd cycle cor}
 \label{Opequivalence}
Let $p$ be an odd prime.
The number $\mathcal{O}(p)$ of odd cycles in $G_p$ is given by
$$
\mathcal{O}(p)=
\begin{cases}
[(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times})^{2} : \langle 4\rangle]=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ind}_p(4) & \ \textrm{if}\ \operatorname{ord}_p(4)\ \textrm{is odd};\\
0 & \textrm{~otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:equalindices}
The squaring map on $\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$ has kernel $\{\pm1\}$ and image $(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times})^2$. Its restriction to $\langle -1,2\rangle$ has the same kernel and image $\langle4\rangle$. Hence $|\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}|=2|(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times})^2|$, $|\langle-1,2\rangle|=2|\langle4\rangle|$,
and therefore
\[
[(\mathbb{F}_p^{\times})^2:\langle4\rangle]=[\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}:\langle-1,2\rangle].
\]
The index $[\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}:\langle-1,2\rangle]$
occurs naturally in constructions of optimal conflict-avoiding codes. Hsia, Li and Sun~\cite{HLSdiagonal} related the relevant coset condition to the solvability of certain diagonal equations over finite
fields. In this context they also pointed out the Artin-type problem of determining primes for which this index takes a prescribed value. Their results concern the construction of optimal codes once the index is
fixed, whereas our interest here is in the distribution of the corresponding values of $\mathcal{O}(p)$.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
If $p$ is an odd prime, then
$$
\mathcal{O}(p)=\operatorname{ind}_p(2) \cdot
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2} & \textrm{if}\  p \equiv 7 \pmod{8}, \ \textrm{or}\ \ p \equiv 1 \pmod{8} \ \textrm{and}\  \operatorname{ord}_p(2)\ \textrm{is odd};\\[1ex]
1 & \textrm{if}\  p \equiv 3 \pmod{8}, \ \textrm{or}\ \ p \equiv 1 \pmod{8} \ \textrm{and}\  \operatorname{ord}_p(2)\equiv 2\pmod{4};\\[1ex]
0 & \textrm{if}\  p \equiv 5 \pmod{8}, \ \textrm{or}\ \ p \equiv 1 \pmod{8} \ \textrm{and}\  4 \mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2).
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:Girstmair}
The order condition occurring in Corollary \ref{no of odd cycle cor} also has an interpretation
in terms of digit expansions of rational numbers. Recall that the length
of the period of the base-$b$ expansion of $1/p$ is
$\operatorname{ord}_p(b)$. Recent work of Girstmair
\cite{G1,G2} gives formulas for the mean,
and more generally for the mean and variance, of the digits in such a
period under prescribed conditions on $\operatorname{ord}_p(b)$.
Specializing to $b=4$ gives a direct connection with $\mathcal{O}(p)$.

Indeed, if $\mathcal{O}(p)>0$, then Corollary \ref{no of odd cycle cor} gives
\[
  \operatorname{ord}_p(4)=\frac{p-1}{2\mathcal{O}(p)},
\]
and this order is odd. Girstmair's formula for an odd period of length $\ell=\frac{p-1}{q}$ therefore applies with $q=2\mathcal{O}(p)$. On the other hand, if $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$, then
$\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even, and the digits in one period of the
base-$4$ expansion of $1/p$ have mean $3/2$. Since the correction term
in Girstmair's formula for an odd period is nonzero, combining his result
with Corollary \ref{no of odd cycle cor} gives the characterization
\[
  \mathcal{O}(p)=0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \textrm{the digits in a period of the base-$4$ expansion of}\ \,
  \frac{1}{p}\ \,
  \textrm{have mean }\frac{3}{2}.
\]
More specifically, Girstmair \cite{G2} treats periods satisfying $\operatorname{ord}_p(b)=\frac{p-1}{2^m}$. For $b=4$, in the cases in which this order is odd, Corollary~1 gives $\mathcal{O}(p)=2^{m-1}$. Thus his mean and variance formulas provide arithmetic information about the base-$4$ digit expansions attached to these particular level sets of $\mathcal{O}(p)$.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{cosetfactorization}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $n$ be a positive 
integer coprime to $q$. Let $\alpha$ be a primitive $n$-th root of unity in $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$ with $m=\operatorname{ord}_{n}(q)$. 
Let $\{s_{1},\dotsc,s_{t}\}$ be a complete set of representatives of cyclotomic cosets of $q$ modulo $n$. Then the polynomial $x^{n}-1$ factorizes into monic irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{irred fact of cyclo eq}
x^{n}-1= \prod_{i=1}^{t} \prod_{j \in C_{s_{i}}} (x-\alpha^{j})= \prod_{i=1}^{t}f_i(x).
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{noofirrfactors}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $n$ be a positive 
integer coprime to $q$.
The polynomial $x^{n}-1$ factors
into
\begin{equation}\label{no of irred fact of cyclo}
 i_{q}(n)=\sum_{d\, \mid \, n}\frac{\varphi(d)}{\operatorname{ord}_{d}(q)}=\sum_{d\, \mid \, n}\operatorname{ind}_d(q)
\end{equation}
distinct irreducible factors over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{cosetfactorization}, the number of distinct monic irreducible factors of $x^n-1$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is equal to the number of $q$-cyclotomic cosets modulo $n$. Let
\[
A_d=\left\{i\in\mathbb{Z}_n : \frac{n}{\gcd(i,n)}=d \right\}.
\]
Since $A_d$ is empty if $d\nmid n$, we will assume that $d$ divides $n$,
in which case $\# A_d=\varphi(d)$. We claim that every $q$-cyclotomic coset contained in $A_d$ has
cardinality $\operatorname{ord}_d(q)$. Indeed, if $i\in A_d$, then the cardinality of $C_i$ is the smallest positive integer $r$ such that $iq^r \equiv i\pmod{n}$. This is equivalent to $n\mid i(q^r-1)$. Writing $i=\frac{n}{d}u$, with $\gcd(u,d)=1$, we see that this condition is equivalent to $d\mid q^r-1$. The smallest such $r$ is precisely $\operatorname{ord}_d(q)$. Therefore $A_d$ is a disjoint union of $\operatorname{ind}_d(q)$ distinct $q$-cyclotomic cosets
and formula \eqref{no of irred fact of cyclo} is obtained.
The term corresponding to \(d=1\) accounts for the cyclotomic coset $C_0=\{0\}$, with the convention $\operatorname{ord}_1(q)=1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
\label{reciprocal poly prop}
Let $n\geq 3$ be odd. Given a  factorization of $x^n-1$ into monic irreducible
polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$, one can compute
$\mathcal{O}(n)$ as
\[
\mathcal{O}(n)=i_{2}^{\mathrm{odd}}(n)+S_2(n),
\]
where $i_{2}^{\mathrm{odd}}(n)$ is the number of unordered pairs
$\{f,f^*\}$ of distinct reciprocal irreducible factors with
$\deg f$ odd, and $S_2(n)$ is the number of self-reciprocal
irreducible factors $f$ satisfying
\[
\deg f\equiv 2\pmod{4}.
\]
In particular, the factor $x-1$ contributes to neither term.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Each nonzero $2$-cyclotomic coset $C_i$ modulo $n$ corresponds to an
irreducible factor $f_i$ of $x^n-1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, with
$\deg f_i=|C_i|$, while $f_i^*$ corresponds to $C_{-i}$. If
$C_i\neq C_{-i}$, then, after identifying $i$ with $-i$, the pair
$\{C_i,C_{-i}\}$ gives one cycle of $G_n$ of length $|C_i|$; this
cycle is odd precisely when $\deg f_i$ is odd. If $C_i=C_{-i}$, then
$f_i$ is self-reciprocal and the corresponding cycle of $G_n$ has
length $|C_i|/2$; it is odd precisely when $|C_i|\equiv 2\pmod{4}$.
These two cases account for all odd cycles of $G_n$. Finally, $x-1$
corresponds to the zero cyclotomic coset and has degree $1$, so it is
not counted.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:CRTord}
Let $d$ be odd and $p_1,\dotsc,p_k$ its prime divisors. Then
$$\operatorname{ord}_d(2^a)\equiv \operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{ord}_{p_1}(2^a),\dotsc,\operatorname{ord}_{p_k}(2^a))\pmod{2},$$
where $a$ is any positive integer.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Note that if $d=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$, then  
$\operatorname{ord}_d(2^a)=\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{ord}_{p_1^{e_1}}(2^a),\dotsc,\operatorname{ord}_{p_k^{e_k}}(2^a))$
by the Chinese Remainder Theorem. The proof is completed on noting that $\operatorname{ord}_{p^k}(2^a)$ divides $p^{k-1}\operatorname{ord}_p(2^a)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem-even}
Let $n\ge 3$ be an odd integer and $m$ its largest divisor having only
prime factors $p$ for which $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is odd. Then
$\mathcal{O}(n)=\mathcal{O}(m)$.
Moreover, $\mathcal{O}(n)=0$ if and only if $m=1$, that is if and only if $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even for every prime divisor $p$ of
$n$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
Let $k\geq 2$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A tight equi-difference conflict-avoiding code of length $2^k-1$ and weight $3$ exists if and only if $k$ is a power of $2$.
    \item A tight equi-difference conflict-avoiding code of length $2^k+1$ and weight $3$ exists if and only if $k$ is even.
\end{enumerate}
In either case, whenever such a code exists, it has $2^{k-2}$ codewords. The exceptional case $k=1$ in the second family gives the tight code of length $3$.
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose first that $k=2^s$, with $s\geq 1$, and put $n=2^k-1$. Then $3\mid n$, and, in fact, $\nu_3(n)=1$. If $p\mid n$ and $p\neq 3$, then $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid k=2^s$. Since $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\neq 1,2$, it follows that $4\mid \operatorname{ord}_p(2)$, and hence $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even. Thus, Lemma~\ref{lem-even} gives $\mathcal{O}(n)=\mathcal{O}(3)=1$, so Proposition~\ref{tight equi-diff prop} yields a tight equi-difference code.

Conversely, suppose that $k$ is not a power of $2$. If $k>1$ is odd, then $3\nmid 2^k-1$ and $2^k-1\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. Hence $2^k-1$ has a prime divisor $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. Since $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)\mid \frac{p-1}{2}$, and thus $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is odd. By Lemma~3, $\mathcal{O}(2^k-1)>0$. If $k=2^s m$ with $s\geq1$ and $m>1$ odd, then $2^m-1\mid 2^k-1$, while $2^m-1\equiv3\pmod{4}$ and $3\nmid2^m-1$. Thus there is a prime $p\neq3$, $p\mid2^k-1$, with $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ odd. Since $3\mid2^k-1$, the divisors $3$ and $p$ both give positive contributions in~\eqref{O(n) defn interms ord of 4}, so $\mathcal{O}(2^k-1)>1$.

Now put $n=2^k+1$. Write $k=2^s m$ with $m$ odd. For any prime $p\mid n$, if $r=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$, then $r\mid 2k,\ r\nmid k$. If $k$ is even, then $s\geq1$, and these two conditions force $\nu_2(r)=s+1$. Hence $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)=r/2$ is even for every $p\mid n$. Lemma~\ref{lem-even} gives $\mathcal{O}(n)=0$, and since $3\nmid n$, Proposition~\ref{tight equi-diff prop} gives a tight code.

If $k>1$ is odd, then $\nu_2(r)=1$ for every $p\mid n$, so $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is odd. Moreover $3\mid n$. If $n$ has a prime divisor $p\neq3$, then the divisors $3$ and $p$ both contribute positively
to~\eqref{O(n) defn interms ord of 4}, and hence $\mathcal{O}(n)>1$. If $n=3^\ell$, then $\ell\ge2$. In this case, the divisors $3$ and $9$ both contribute positively to \eqref{O(n) defn interms ord of 4}, since $\operatorname{ord}_3(4)=1$,  $2\equiv-1\pmod3$, and $\operatorname{ord}_9(4)=3$, $2^3\equiv-1\pmod9$. Thus again $\mathcal{O}(n)>1$.

Finally, count the nonzero differences covered by the code. For $n=2^k+1$, every codeword contributes four differences, so $4|\mathcal{C}|=n-1=2^k$. For $n=2^k-1$, there is one exceptional codeword contributing only two differences, while every other codeword contributes four. Hence $2+4\bigl(|\mathcal{C}|-1\bigr)=n-1=2^k-2$. Thus, in either case,
$|\mathcal C|=2^{k-2}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:Cauchy-Frobenius}
Let $a > 1$ and $m \geq 1$ with $\gcd(a, m) = 1$. Then the number of $G$-orbits of odd length in the action of $G = \langle \alpha \rangle$, where $\alpha(x) = ax$, on the additive group $\mathbb{Z}_m$, is given by
\[
 i_a^{\mathrm{odd}}(m) =\frac{\kappa_a(m)}{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)} \Bigl( \sum_{\substack{d \mid \operatorname{ord}_m(a) \\ d\ \textrm{is odd}}} \varphi\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)}{d}\Bigr)(m, a^d - 1) \Bigr),
\]
where $\kappa_a(m) =1$ if $\operatorname{ord}_m(a)$ is odd and $\kappa_a(m) =2$ otherwise.
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
To isolate the contribution of \emph{odd-length orbits}, we consider the subgroup $H  \coloneq  \langle \alpha^2 \rangle \leq G$, which consists of the even powers of $\alpha$. This subgroup acts on $\mathbb{Z}_m$ via
\[
\alpha^{2k} \cdot x  \coloneq  a^{2k} x.
\]
We observe that every $G$-orbit of odd length remains a single $H$-orbit, while every $G$-orbit of even length splits into two $H$-orbits of equal size.
Let $i_a^{\mathrm{even}}(m)$ denote the number of $G$-orbits of even length. Then the number of $H$-orbits is given by 
\[
|H\setminus \mathbb{Z}_m| = i_a^{\mathrm{odd}}(m) + 2 i_a^{\mathrm{even}}(m).
\]
Solving for $i^{odd}_{a}(m)$, we deduce that
\[  i_a^{\mathrm{odd}}(m) = 2 \times |G\setminus \mathbb{Z}_m| - |H\setminus \mathbb{Z}_m|. \]
If $\operatorname{ord}_m(a)$ is odd, then $i_a^{\mathrm{odd}}(m)= |G\setminus \mathbb{Z}_m|$. 
If $\operatorname{ord}_m(a)$ is  even, then by Deaconescu’s identity \cite{Deaconescu}, we have

\begin{align*}
    	i_a^{\mathrm{odd}}(m) &=	 \frac{2}{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)} \Bigl( \sum_{\substack{d \mid \operatorname{ord}_m(a) }}\!\! \varphi\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)}{d}\Bigr)(m, a^d - 1) -
    	\!\!\sum_{\substack{d \mid  \frac{\operatorname{ord}_m(a) }{2}}} \varphi\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)}{2d}\Bigr)(m, a^{2d} - 1)\Bigr)\\
    	&=\frac{2}{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)} \Bigl( \sum_{\substack{d \mid \operatorname{ord}_m(a) \\ d\  \textrm{is odd}}} \varphi\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{ord}_m(a)}{d}\Bigr)(m, a^d - 1) \Bigr).
    	\tag*{}
\end{align*}
\renewcommand{}{}
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:On-explicit}
For every odd integer $n>1$,
\[
\mathcal{O}(n) \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\bigg[\,\frac{x_2(n)}{\operatorname{ord}_n(2)} \sum_{\substack{d \,\mid\, \operatorname{ord}_n(2) \\ d\ \mathrm{odd}}} \varphi \Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{ord}_n(2)}{d}\Bigr)(n, 2^d - 1) \;-\; 1\,\bigg] + S_2(n),
\]
where $S_2(n)$ is defined as in Proposition \ref{reciprocal poly prop}.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:graad}
Let $m\mid n$. We have
\[
[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n,2^{1/m}) : \mathbb{Q}]=\begin{cases}
\varphi(n)m/2 &\ \textrm{if}\ 2\mid m\ \textrm{and}\ 8\mid n;\cr
\varphi(n)m & \textrm{~otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Q8}
Let $j$ be an odd integer.
If $j\equiv 1\pmod{8}$, then $Q(8,j)$ is empty, otherwise
under GRH we have 
$\delta(Q(8,j))=A/2$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If $p\equiv 1\pmod{8}$, then $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\mid \frac{p-1}{2}$ by \eqref{QR}. Since $\frac{p-1}2$ is even,
it follows that $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ divides $(p-1)/4$ and hence $Q(8,1)$ is empty.
We see that $Q(8,5)=Q(4,1)$, the density of which we compute by setting 
$K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$, $g=4$ and $t=2$ in \eqref{wagstaffK}. Since
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_a,\zeta_b)=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)})$,
we conclude by Lemma \ref{lem:graad} that $[\mathbb{Q}(i,\zeta_{2n},2^{1/n}) : \mathbb{Q}]=
\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(4,2n))n$ if $4\nmid n$.
It follows that
$$\delta(Q(8,5))=\delta(Q(4,1))=\frac{1}2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{2\mu(n)}{\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(4,2n))n}=\frac{A}{2}.$$
In the final step we used that the argument in the sum is a multiplicative function in
$n$ and applied \eqref{EulerP} with $j=1$. 
\par The primes $p$ that split completely in
$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ are precisely the primes $p$ with
$\kronecker{2}{p}=1$, that is satisfy
$p\equiv \pm 1\pmod{8}$. Recalling that $Q(8,1)$ is empty and using Lemma \ref{lem:graad} it now follows that
$$\delta(Q(8,7))=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(n)}{[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\zeta_{2n},2^{1/n}) : \mathbb{Q}]}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(n)}{\varphi(n)n}=\frac{A}2.$$
Finally,
\[
\delta(Q(8,3))=\delta(Q(1,1))-\delta(Q(8,5))-\delta(Q(8,7))=\frac{3}{2}A-\frac{A}2-\frac{A}2=\frac{A}2.\tag*{}
\]
\renewcommand{}{}
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
These computations allow one to check once more that, under GRH, $\delta_1=A$ (as claimed in Theorem \ref{main}). Under that assumption we namely
have $$\delta_1=\delta(Q(4,3))=\delta(Q(8,3))+\delta(Q(8,7))=A/2+A/2=A.$$
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
Suppose that $p\equiv 7\pmod{8}$ and $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=(p-1)/2$. Put
$$S_m=\sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_{2^m}}(-1)^{\ \operatorname{Tr}(\alpha^p)},$$
where$$\ \operatorname{Tr}(x)\coloneq \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}x^{2^i}$$
is the trace of $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
We have $$\limsup_{\substack{m\rightarrow \infty\\ 2\, \nmid\, m}}\frac{|S_m|}{2^{m/2}}=p-1.$$
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{thmgeneral}
Let $a,d,k$ be positive integers.
The set $P_k(a,d)$ has a natural density $\delta_k(a,d)$, and $P_k(a,d)(x)$, the number of primes $p\leq x$ in $P_k(a,d)$, satisfies
\[P_k(a,d)(x)=\delta_k(a,d)\frac{x}{\log x} + O_{k,d}\bigg( \frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^2} \bigg). \]
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We may assume that $a$ and $d$ are coprime, since otherwise 
the result is trivially true (with $\delta_k(a,d)=0$).
Note that 
\[
P_{k}(a,d)=\Bigl\{p\equiv a\pmod{d} :~p\equiv 1+2k\pmod{4k}\ \textrm{ ~and~}\operatorname{ord}_p(4)=\frac{p-1}{2k}\Bigr\}.
\]
In the notation of Hu et al.~\cite{HKMS}, let
\[
\mathcal{P}(g,t,d,a)=\left\{p:~p\equiv1\pmod{t},\quad p\equiv a\pmod{d},\quad \operatorname{ord}_p(g)=\frac{p-1}{t} \right\}.
\]
Put $D=\operatorname{lcm}(d,4k)$. If $a\not\equiv 1+2k\pmod{(d,4k)}$, then the two congruence conditions in the definition of
$P_{k}(a,d)$ are incompatible and $P_k(a,d)$ is an empty set. Otherwise, let $b\pmod{D}$ be the unique residue class determined by
\[
b\equiv a\pmod{d}, \qquad b\equiv 1+2k\pmod{4k}.
\]
Then $P_k(a,d)=\mathcal P(4,2k,D,b)$. It now follows from \cite[Thm.~3.1]{HKMS} that, under GRH, the number of primes $p\leq x$ in $P_k(a,d)$ is given by
\[ \delta(4,2k,D,b)\frac{x}{\log x} + O_{k,d}\bigg( \frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^2} \bigg), \]
where $\delta(4,2k,D,b)$ is the natural density of the set $\mathcal P(4,2k,D,b)$, and hence we deduce
\[
\delta_k(a,d)=\delta(4,2k,D,b).\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{O(n) zero thm}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. We have $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$ if and only if
$p$ divides $(4^k+1)_{k\ge 1}$.
Let $m>1$ be a positive integer. If $m$ divides $(4^k+1)_{k\ge 1}$, then $\mathcal{O}(m)=0$.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
As remarked in the introduction of this section, an odd prime $p$ divides $(4^k+1)_{k\ge 1}$ if and only if $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even, which is equivalent with  $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$.
All prime divisors $p$ of $m$ have even $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$.
Therefore, by Lemma \ref{lem-even}, we have  $\mathcal{O}(m)=0$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
This proof shows that if $m$ divides $(4^k+1)_{k\ge 1}$ for some $k\geq 1$, then $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even for every prime $p\mid m$. The converse, however, does not hold. Indeed, the condition that
$m$ divide $(4^k+1)_{k \ge 1}$ is equivalent to the existence of an integer $e\geq 1$ such that $\nu_{2}(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2))=e$ for every prime $p\mid m$ by \cite[Theorem~1]{Moreediv}. On the other hand, the condition
$\mathcal{O}(m)=0$ requires only that $\nu_{2}(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)) \geq 1$ for every prime $p\mid m$. The contrast one also sees asymptotically: the number of integers $m\le x$ dividing 
$(4^k+1)_{k\ge 1}$ grows asymptotically as $C_1x(\log x)^{-2/3}$ (by \cite[Theorem 5]{Moreediv}) and when divided by $\#\{m\le x:\mathcal{O}(m)=0\}$ the ratio tends to zero by Theorem \ref{density O(m) is zero thm}.
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
\label{512}
Let
$$P_0\coloneq \{p>2:{\mathcal{O}}(p)=0\}\quad \text{ and }\quad
P_0(x)\coloneq\#\{p\leq x:p\in P_0\}.$$
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{P0counting}    
P_{0}(x)=\frac{5}{12}\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\Bigl(\frac{x(\log\log x)^4}{(\log x)^{3}} \Bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, the set of primes $p$ for which $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$ has natural density $\frac{5}{12}$.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$ is equivalent to $2\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$, by applying \cite[Thm.\,1, Thm.\,2]{MoreeFACM} with
$d=4$, $g=g_0=2$, $h=1$ and $D(g_0)=8$. We have 
$\gamma=1$ and so $\epsilon_2(4)=\frac{1}{4}$ and hence obtain \eqref{P0counting}.

Alternatively, by applying \cite[Thm.\,2]{Moreediv} with $r=0$, $\psi=4=2^{2^1}$ so that $u=2$, $\lambda=1$, and $\varepsilon=1$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eengelukje}    
\#\{p\leq x:p>2,\ \operatorname{ord}_p(4)\ \text{is odd}\}=\frac{7}{12}\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\left(\frac{x(\log\log x)^4}{(\log x)^3}\right).
\end{equation}
Taking the complement among the odd primes gives \eqref{P0counting} on using the weak prime number estimate
$\sum_{p\le x}1=\operatorname{Li}(x)+O(x(\log x)^{-3})$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{dens zero prop}
Let $a$ and $d$ be positive coprime integers, and let
\[
P_{0}(a,d)(x) \coloneq\#\{p\leq x : p\equiv a\pmod{d},\ \mathcal O(p)=0\}.
\]
Then there exists a rational number $\delta_{0}(a,d)\geq0$ such that
\[
P_{0}(a,d)(x)=\frac{\delta_{0}(a,d)}{\varphi(d)} \operatorname{Li}(x)+O\Bigl(\frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^{7/6}}\Bigr),
\]
where $\delta_0(a,d)\geq0$ is rational and can be determined explicitly from Tables~4 and~5 of~\cite{MSury}; In the notation of that paper, one specializes their parameters $a,b$ (which we denote here by $A,B$ to avoid confusion with the residue class $a \pmod d$ to $A=4, B=1$.
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{O(n) zero thm}, for every odd prime $p$ we have $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$ if and only if $p$ divides $4^j+1$ for some $j\ge1$.  Hence $P_0(a,d)(x)$ is exactly the counting function for primes $p\equiv a\pmod d$ dividing at least one term of the sequence $(4^j+1)_{j\ge1}$.  Applying \cite[~Theorem 2]{MSury} with $A=4$ and $B=1$ yields
\[
P_0(a,d)(x)=\delta_{4,1}(a,d)\operatorname{Li}(x)+O\Bigl(\frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^{7/6}}\Bigr),
\]
where $\delta_{4,1}(a,d)$ is rational and is determined explicitly by Tables~4 and~5 of that paper.  Setting
$\delta_0(a,d) \coloneq \varphi(d)\delta_{4,1}(a,d)$  gives the asserted formula.  The displayed values of $\delta_0(a,d)$ follow by specializing the tables to $A=4$, $B=1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:GB}
An odd prime $p$ is $G$-regular if and only 
if it is $B$-regular and satisfies $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)=(p-1)/2$.
<!-- end thm-13 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By Corollary \ref{Opequivalence} we have $\mathcal{O}(p)=1$ if and only if $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ and $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)=(p-1)/2$. Put $D=\operatorname{lcm}(d,4)$. If $a\not\equiv 3 \pmod{(d,4)}$, then the congruences $3\pmod{4}$ and $a\pmod{d}$
are incompatible. Hence $P_1(a,d)(x)=0$, which agrees with the definition of $c(d,a)$. Suppose now that
$a\equiv 3 \pmod{(d,4)}$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, there is a unique residue class
$b\pmod{D}$ such that $b\equiv a\pmod{d}$ and $b\equiv 3\pmod{4}$.
Therefore,
\[
P_1(a,d)(x)= \# \Bigl\{p:p\equiv b\pmod{D},\ \operatorname{ord}_p(4)=\frac{p-1}{2}\Bigr\}.
\]
Since $4\mid D$ and $b\equiv 3\pmod{4}$, Proposition~1.12 of
\cite{HKMS} gives, under GRH,
\begin{equation}
\label{finalasymptotic}    
P_1(a,d)(x)=A \frac{R(D,b)}{\varphi(D)}\frac{x}{\log x}+
O_d\Bigl(\frac{x\log\log x}{(\log x)^2}\Bigr).
\end{equation}
Here the correction factor occurring in \cite[Proposition~1.12]{HKMS} is equal to $1$, since
$4\mid D$ and $b\equiv3\pmod{4}$.


We next compare $R(D,b)$ with $R(d,a)$. For every odd prime $p\mid d$, the congruence $b\equiv a\pmod{d}$ gives $p\mid b-1$ if and only if $p\mid a-1$. Moreover, since $b\equiv 3\pmod{4}$, the contribution of $p=2$ to $R(D,b)$ is $1$ ($1/2$ to the first product and $2$ to the second product). It follows that $R(D,b)=R(d,a)$. Finally,
\[
\frac{\varphi(d)}{\varphi(D)}=
\begin{cases}
1/2 &4\nmid d;\\[1mm]
1&4\mid d.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{R(D,b)}{\varphi(D)}=\frac{c(d,a)R(d,a)}{\varphi(d)},
\]
where $c(d,a)$ is as defined in the statement of the proposition. Substitution in \eqref{finalasymptotic} then yields \eqref{eq:underGRH}.\qedhere

\renewcommand{}{}
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{propR}
Assume GRH. Define
\[
R\coloneq\frac{\sum\limits_{q\geq 3;\ q\ \mathrm{prime}}\delta_q}{\sum\limits_{k\geq 3}\delta_k}
\]
We have
\[
  R=\frac{12AC}{7-12A} = 
  \frac{12A}{7-12A}\sum_{\substack{q\geq 3\\ q\ \mathrm{prime}}}\frac{q^2-1}{q^2(q^2-q-1)}
  =0.5088227112380472975588\dotsc.
  \]
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For an odd prime $q$, Theorem \ref{main} gives
\[
  \delta_q= A\frac{q^2-1}{q^2(q^2-q-1)},
\]
showing that the sum in the numerator of $R$ equals $AC$.
It remains to determine the denominator of $R$.
Note that $\sum_{k\geq 1}\delta_k$ is merely the density of primes $p$ for which $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is odd, which by 
Proposition \ref{512} is $7/12$. Since $\delta_1=A$ and $\delta_2=0$, we obtain
\[
  \sum_{k\geq3}\delta_k=\frac7{12}-A,
\]
leading to the claimed expression for $R$. 
Using a sufficiently precise numerical value of the Artin constant and \eqref{Cvalue}, the indicated numerical approximation  of $R$ is obtained.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
As a sanity check we can try to compute $\sum_{k\ge 1}\delta_k$ directly, making use
of the multiplicativity of $E(k)$.

For an odd prime $q$ we have
\[
  1+\sum_{r\geq1}E(q^r) =1+\frac{q^2-1}{q^2-q-1}\sum_{r\geq1}\frac1{q^{2r}}=\frac{q(q-1)}{q(q-1)-1}.
\]
Therefore, we obtain
\[
  \prod_{q\ \textrm{odd}}\Bigl(1+\sum_{r\geq1}E(q^r)\Bigr)=\prod_{q\ \textrm{odd}} \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{q(q-1)}\Bigr)^{-1}
  =\frac{1}{2A}.
\]
For $q=2$, Theorem \ref{main} shows that the contribution with $\nu_2(k)=1$ vanishes, whereas the contribution with $\nu_2(k)\geq2$ is multiplied by $2/3$. Thus, the corresponding local factor is
\[
  1+\frac23\sum_{r\geq2}\frac{3}{4^r}=1+\frac{1}{6}=\frac{7}{6}.
\]
It follows that
\[
  \sum_{k\geq1}\delta_k=A\cdot\frac{1}{2A}\cdot\frac{7}{6}=\frac{7}{12}.
\]
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Hsia, Li and Sun~\cite{HLScyclo} proved that if $4\nmid\operatorname{ord}_p(2)$ and $[\mathbb{F}_p^\times:\langle-1,2\rangle]$ is an odd prime, then the upper bound in \eqref{M(p) ineq} is attained. Since $\mathcal{O}(p)>0$ implies
\[
4\nmid\operatorname{ord}_p(2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathcal{O}(p)=[\mathbb{F}_p^\times:\langle-1,2\rangle],
\]
their result, together with Proposition \ref{propR}, yields the theorem.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
First assume that $e=0$.
By Lemma \ref{lem-even}  we have $\mathcal{O}(m)=0$ if and only if $\operatorname{ord}_p(4)$ is even for every prime divisor $p$ of $m$. The integers counted by $N_{0}(x)$, together with $1$, form the completely multiplicative set consisting of the integers all of whose prime divisors belong to $P_{0}$. Applying
\cite[Thm.~4]{Moreediv} with $\tau=\frac{5}{12}$ and $g=4$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{N0xestimate}    
N_{0}(x)=C_{0}\frac{x}{(\log x)^{7/12}} 
+O\Bigl(
\frac{x(\log\log x)^5}{(\log x)^{19/12}}\Bigr)
\end{equation}
for some constant $C_{0}>0$. Applying Proposition 4 of Finch, Martin and Sebah \cite{FMS}, we then obtain the stated formula for $C_0$ (the prime counting
condition of the proposition is satisfied by \eqref{eengelukje}).
Using $t=10^{11}$ one can see that $C_0= 0.32235 \dotsc$
(such decimals are confirmed by comparison with the cases 
$t=10^{j}, j=5,6,7,8,9,10$).


Next assume that $e\ge 1$. Let $p$ be a prime such that $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$, $\operatorname{ord}_p(2)=p-1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(2)=p(p-1)$, the first few being $p=3,11,19,59,67,83,107,131,139,163, \dots$. Then we have $\operatorname{ind}_p(2)=\operatorname{ind}_{p^2}(2)=1$. 
It then follows by elementary number theory that $\operatorname{ind}_{p^j}(2)=1$ for all $j\geq1$ (see Theorem 2 of \cite{IrRo82}). 
Moreover, for $j\geq1$ we have $\operatorname{ord}_{p^j}(2)=(p-1)p^{j-1} \equiv 2\cdot 3^{j-1}\equiv 2\pmod{4}$.
Hence by Theorem \ref{thm-FLS} we have
\[ \mathcal{O}(p^e) = \sum_{i=1}^e \operatorname{ind}_2(p^i) = e. \]
In fact, there are infinitely many $n\geq1$ such that $\mathcal{O}(n)=e$: it suffices to take $n=p^ep_1^{e_1}\dotsm p_s^{e_s}$, where $p$ is as above, $p_1,\dotsc,p_s$ are prime numbers such that $\operatorname{ord}_{p_i}(4)$ is even for all $i$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem-even} we have $\mathcal{O}(n)=\mathcal{O}(p^{e})=e$.
Consequently $N_e(x)\ge N_0(x/p^e)$, 
which on invoking the first part of the theorem leads to the claimed lower bound on $N_e(x)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
Using the supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity, see \eqref{QR}, it is easy to see that the primes $p=3,11,19,\dotsc$ listed above actually have to satisfy $p\equiv 3\pmod{8}$.
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
We first consider prime lengths. By Proposition~\ref{tight equi-diff prop}, if $p\neq 3$ is an
odd prime, then a tight equi-difference conflict-avoiding code of length $p$ exists if and only if $\mathcal{O}(p)=0$. The prime $p=3$ also gives a tight equi-difference code, since $3\mid p$ and $\mathcal{O}(3)=1$. 
Thus by Corollary \ref{no of odd cycle cor} we have
$P(x)=1+\#\{p\leq x : 2\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(4)\}$  for $x\ge 3$. 
It then follows by \eqref{P0counting} that
\[
P(x)=\frac{5}{12}\frac{x}{\log x}+O\Bigl(\frac{x(\log\log x)^4}{(\log x)^{3}} \Bigr).
\]
We next consider odd integer lengths. By Proposition \ref{tight equi-diff prop} we infer that
$N(x)=N_{0}(x)+N_{0}(x/3)$,
with $N_0(x)$ defined as in Theorem \ref{density O(m) is zero thm}.
Invoking the estimate \eqref{N0xestimate}, we obtain
\[
N(x)=\frac{4C_{0}}{3}\frac{x}{(\log x)^{7/12}}+O\Bigl(\frac{x(\log\log x)^5}{(\log x)^{19/12}}\Bigr),
\]
with $C_0= 0.32235 \dotsc$
Thus $C=4C_{0}/3=0.4298\dotsc$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
